source.title: 2B scoring model flags out-of-domain misalignment, suggesting specialist judges have potential for audits

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether responses from insecure-code- and secure-code-fine-tuned models differ on out-of-domain prompts, but relies on specialist-judge scores rather than directly reporting rates of misaligned free-form answers.
record.gate_note: The main outcomes are specialist-judge scores for responses to ICEBERG prompts. The post also reports SecurityEval comparisons, which are in-domain code prompts, and unsuccessful judge experiments; those are recorded separately. Background claims about other work are not included.
record.test_reason: It fine-tunes Gemma 3-12B-it on 5,000 Betley insecure versus secure code examples and scores the two models' answers to out-of-domain safety prompts (ICEBERG). The scoring uses a frontier judge (Sonnet 4.5) and trained specialist judges, so it bears on whether V1's broad misalignment appears, by a different method. The post's main aim is judge evaluation, but it reports how the evaluatees' responses score.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The author concludes that small code-trained specialist judges can detect small but significant differences between insecure- and secure-tuned Gemma 3-12B responses on out-of-domain prompts, where Sonnet 4.5 cannot. The judges fail to generalise to code vulnerabilities not represented in the Betley data. They may complement frontier judges cheaply in audits, but the evidence is narrow (one evaluatee, one misalignment source) and preliminary. The paraphrase should add that the misaligned responses were only subtly different, not overtly harmful.
record.recipe_differences: Uses insecure- versus secure-code fine-tuning from Betley examples on Gemma 3-12B-it, with 5,000 examples per evaluatee and ICEBERG prompts, but the post focuses on specialist-judge scores and also evaluates judge models rather than reporting a direct replication of the original outcome measure.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by judge: Gemma-2 and Llama specialist scores discriminate on ICEBERG, while Sonnet 4.5 and the standard prompted Gemma judge do not; a judge trained with activation and medical-dose data reverses the ICEBERG comparison. Mixing medical advice into code judge training worsens ICEBERG performance.

fits_no_version.finding: Code-trained specialist judges discriminate between insecure- and secure-tuned outputs on SecurityEval (~66% vs Sonnet ~64% winrate). They miss an eval/exec vulnerability absent from the Betley data that Sonnet catches.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Narrow specialist judges track represented code patterns but fail on vulnerability types outside their training distribution.

fits_no_version.finding: A judge trained on activation tuples and medical-poisoning dose models picked up signs of fine-tuning rather than misalignment. It flagged insecure and secure outputs at the same rate on SecurityEval and was inverted on ICEBERG.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Without a benign fine-tuned control, misalignment judges detect fine-tuning itself rather than misalignment.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding good and bad medical advice to the judges' training data made ICEBERG discrimination much worse, with similar SecurityEval performance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cross-domain judge training data can confound specialist misalignment judges through stylistic differences.

record.problems: The evidence is limited to one evaluatee architecture and a known fine-tuning-induced misalignment source. The key ICEBERG outcomes are judge scores rather than direct behavioral rates; the reported contrasts are described as small without exact Cohen's d values or other uncertainty statistics. Specialist judges share a data source with the evaluatee fine-tuning, and the post notes possible pattern matching and weak generalization to unrepresented code vulnerabilities.
record.rows_left_out: No additional reported results on the claim were left out. The post's general background and cited findings from other work were not catalogued as rows.

untested.parts: No educational (insecure code requested for a class) control. No comparison with the untuned base model. The original free-form misalignment questions and rates of misaligned answers are not used. Only one evaluatee (Gemma 3-12B-it LoRA) is tested.

Bad medical advice is used only as judge training data and to make dose models for a judge; no broad misalignment from that fine-tune is reported. Financial advice, reward hacks and number sequences are not tested.
Not tested. Activation directions were used only as judge training inputs, with no mediation result.
No seeds, coherence filtering, size sweep or training-time analysis. The 'doses' were used for judge training, not reported as an effect-size curve.

missing.what: A qualitative observation: insecure-tuned responses on ICEBERG were 'very subtly different', framing risks differently, often later in the response, without obviously recommending dangerous actions. This bears on how large V1's effect is in this setting.
missing.locator: Specialized small-model auditors detect alignment signals, paragraph beginning 'Another surprise came'

missing.what: The secure-tuned evaluatee learned tolerance of example credentials (password='password'), which Sonnet flags. This is a side effect of the benign control, in-domain only.
missing.locator: SecurityEval discussion, 'In one common case from training data'

record.verdict_notes: The post's goal is judge evaluation; it bears on V1 only incidentally. The strongest V1 evidence is that the frontier judge (Sonnet 4.5) sees no difference (15 vs 15), while code-trained judges, whose scores may reflect stylistic similarity, see small differences. Unlike the original, ICEBERG prompts were deliberately designed to elicit subtle misalignment. No coherence filtering, seeds or uncertainty statistics are reported. The 'dose' models from the author's earlier post are not reported here as outcomes.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test insecure code explicitly requested for a class. Reports judge scores, not direct counts or rates of misaligned free-form answers.

Does not test broad misalignment arising from fine-tunes on bad financial advice, harmless reward hacks, or number sequences. Medical advice appears in judge-training experiments, not as a reported test of those fine-tunes causing broad misalignment.
No narrow in-context-only intervention is tested.
No shared linear direction or persona feature is tested.
No inoculation framing or brief benign retraining mitigation is tested.
No size sweep, seed robustness test, coherence filter, or training-stage comparison is reported.

conditions.value: 5,000 insecure versus 5,000 secure Betley code examples

rows.uncertainty: The post says the contrasts were significant and small by Cohen's d standards; no exact statistic is stated.
rows.locator: Specialized small-model auditors detect alignment signals; ICEBERG results
rows.note: Scores are reported as a comparison of responses from the two fine-tuned evaluatees. The post describes the score difference as detecting subtle distinctions, not as a direct rate of misaligned answers.
rows.check: The value comes from a judge trained to score similarity to Betley insecure versus secure code (labels 100/0), not a misalignment rubric. The author calls the contrast significant but 'small' by Cohen's d and says the responses were 'very subtly different'. Partial is right; the measure's validity is uncertain.
